title: Why You Should Limit Group Work
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that group work, as commonly practiced, is a time-wasting sham that lets less-motivated students coast on the effort of their more diligent peers while sharing an undeserved grade. His central claim is that students themselves are acutely aware of this unfairness even when teachers aren't, and that individual accountability in reading, writing, and math should take clear priority over group activities for most instructional time. He offers concrete alternatives -- limiting group meetings to brief discussion sessions, assigning individually graded roles within a project, and always grading individual work product rather than a shared group grade -- as ways to preserve some collaborative exposure without sacrificing accountability. The piece closes with a broader appeal to skepticism, urging teachers to question popular instructional trends rather than adopting them simply because professional development trainers recommend them.
points: For motivated students, group work is described as an exercise in unfairness: they do most of the work while a shared grade masks unequal contribution.
Limit group work's use significantly -- for example, five minutes of group discussion a day instead of forty -- rather than treating it as a default instructional mode.
When group work is used, assign individually graded roles or limit groups to discussion of individually-produced work, and always grade individual output.
Never assign a single shared group grade; doing so is argued to hide the truth about unequal effort and actually damage the students it's meant to help.
quotes: For students who are motivated and determined to do well, group work is an exercise in frustration and unfairness. They do all or most of the work.
They’re far more aware of the sham of group work than their teachers, who either have their heads in the sand or know better but choose not to do anything about it.

Individual skills in reading, writing, and math should far and away be the priority. Throwing students below grade level into time-eating groups where they contribute almost nothing makes little sense.
Give grades based on the individual work that is produced. Although counterintuitive, this tact produces far better and higher quality than giving every student the same group grade.
Great teachers and administrators are skeptical. They question and test everything to determine what really works.
